questions.question: The graph shows changes in conductivity as hydrochloric acid is added to 25 mL of sodium hydroxide solution. Which statement about this titration is correct?
options: The equivalence point occurred when 15 mL of acid was added.
The equivalence point occurred when 25 mL of acid was added.
Neutralisation is incomplete as the conductivity has not reached zero.
The end point occurred when 15 mL of acid was added, and the equivalence point when 25 mL was added.
questions.answer: **A.** Conductivity is a minimum at the equivalence point.

questions.question: The graph shows changes in conductivity as hydrochloric acid is added to 25 mL of sodium hydroxide solution. Given that the concentration of the sodium hydroxide was 0.12 M, what is the concentration of the hydrochloric acid?
How many different structural isomers are there for $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{BrCl}$?
questions.answer: **D.** 1,1-, 2,2-, 1-bromo-2-chloro-, 2-bromo-1-chloro- and 1-bromo-3-chloro- (halogen positions on propane).

questions.question: A 250.0 mL sample of 0.40 M hydrochloric acid is added to 750.0 mL of 0.60 M potassium hydroxide solution. What is the final concentration of hydroxide ions?
How many structurally different products are possible when but-2-ene reacts with $\text{HCl}(g)$?
questions.answer: **A.** But-2-ene is symmetrical, so only 2-chlorobutane forms.

questions.question: $\text{Br}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{IBr}(g)$ has $K_{eq}=1.2\times10^{2}$ at 150 °C. What is $K_c$ for $4\text{IBr}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{Br}_2(g)+2\text{I}_2(g)$ at 150 °C?
questions.answer: **C.** The equation is reversed and doubled: $K=\left(\dfrac{1}{120}\right)^2=6.9\times10^{-5}$.

questions.question: Jennie wants to use a physical property to distinguish between two colourless liquid alcohols, octan-1-ol and propan-1-ol. She should use:
options: density, because propan-1-ol has a much higher density than octan-1-ol.
boiling point, because octan-1-ol has a higher boiling point than propan-1-ol.
electrical conductivity, because octan-1-ol has a higher conductivity than propan-1-ol.
spectroscopy, because it is not possible to distinguish them using other physical properties.
questions.answer: **B.** The longer chain gives stronger dispersion forces.

questions.question: The equilibrium expression for a reaction is $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{H}^+]^6}{[\text{Bi}^{3+}]^2[\text{H}_2\text{S}]^3}$. The reaction could be:
questions.answer: **C.** $\text{H}^+$ is a product, and solid $\text{Bi}_2\text{S}_3$ is omitted from the expression.

questions.question: The indicator HIn is used in a titration between hydrochloric acid and magnesium hydroxide solutions: $\text{HIn}(aq)\ (\text{green})\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{In}^-(aq)\ (\text{purple})$. The indicator is added to 20.0 mL of magnesium hydroxide solution in a conical flask and the acid is added from a burette until the end point. The solutions are of similar concentrations. Which describes the colour of the solution in the flask?
options: It starts green and turns purple after about 10 mL.
It starts green and turns purple after about 40 mL.
It starts purple and turns green after about 10 mL.
It starts purple and turns green after about 40 mL.
questions.answer: **D.** In base the equilibrium lies right (purple). $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ needs two moles of HCl per mole, so about 40 mL.

questions.question: The pH of a solution of HCOOH is 3.0. What is the concentration of the acid if $pK_a=3.75$? (Assume negligible dissociation.)

A spirit burner containing an alcohol (molar mass 74.1 g mol$^{-1}$) heated 200.0 g of water from 23.0 °C to 45.0 °C. The burner's mass fell from 350.75 g to 350.01 g. What is the molar heat of combustion of the alcohol?
The conjugate base of the ammonium ion is:
questions.answer: **A.** A conjugate base has one less proton.

questions.question: 1.0 mL of 10 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid was diluted to 1 L. 100 mL of this solution was then diluted to 1 L. What is the pH of the final solution closest to?

For $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, $K_{eq}=1.75$ at 1000 °C. An equilibrium mixture at 1000 °C has 0.12 M $\text{SO}_2$ and 0.16 M $\text{O}_2$. The equilibrium concentration of $\text{SO}_3$ is:
Which mixture would produce a buffer solution when dissolved in 1.0 L of water?
questions.answer: **B.** Half-neutralisation leaves comparable amounts of the weak acid and its conjugate base.

questions.question: Separate 25.0 mL samples of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ ethanoic acid and 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid are prepared. Which statement is correct?
options: Both will react with 1.00 g of magnesium ribbon at the same rate.
Both have the same electrical conductivity.
The concentration of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is greater in the ethanoic acid.
Both will react completely with 25.0 mL of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution.
questions.answer: **D.** Both contain the same number of moles of acidic hydrogen.

questions.question: Consider the reaction sequence shown. Which row correctly identifies X, Y and Z?
options: X: but-1-ene; Y: (1-butyl) ethanoate; Z: butanoic acid
X: butane; Y: hexanoic acid; Z: butan-1-ol
X: but-2-ene; Y: ethyl butanoate; Z: butanoate
X: cyclobutane; Y: butyl acetate; Z: butanal
questions.answer: **A.** Dehydration gives but-1-ene, esterification gives butyl ethanoate, and oxidation of the primary alcohol gives butanoic acid.

questions.question: Which of the labelled hydrogens in the molecule shown gives a triplet signal in a $^1$H NMR spectrum?
questions.answer: **D.** Hydrogen z has two neighbouring protons (the $\text{CH}_2$ group x).

questions.question: The infrared spectrum of an unknown sample is shown. What is it most likely to be?
questions.answer: **A.** There is a strong C=O absorption and no broad O–H band.

questions.question: The graph shows the boiling points and carbon chain lengths of nine organic compounds A–I: three carboxylic acids, three alkylamines and three amides. Which correctly identifies the groups?
options: Acids: D, E, F; amines: A, B, C; amides: G, H, I
Acids: A, D, G; amines: B, E, H; amides: C, F, I
Acids: B, E, H; amines: C, F, I; amides: A, D, G
Acids: C, E, G; amines: A, F, H; amides: B, D, I
questions.answer: **C.** For a given chain length, boiling point increases from amine to carboxylic acid to amide.

For $\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)+\text{CO}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}_2(g)+\text{H}_2(g)$:

| $\text{CO}_2(g)$ | −393 | 214 |

Determine whether this reaction is spontaneous at 600 K under standard conditions.
questions.answer: $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S=-40-600(-0.042)=-14.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. $\Delta G<0$, so it is spontaneous.

questions.question:
For $\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)+\text{CO}(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{CO}_2(g)+\text{H}_2(g)$:

| | $\Delta H_f^\circ$ (kJ mol$^{-1}$) | $S^\circ$ (J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$) |
|---|---|---|
| CO(g) | −111 | 198 |
| $\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$ | −242 | 189 |
| $\text{CO}_2(g)$ | −393 | 214 |
| $\text{H}_2(g)$ | 0 | 131 |

Given that $\Delta G=0$ at equilibrium, calculate the temperature at which this reaction reaches equilibrium under standard conditions and state when it is spontaneous.
questions.answer: $T=\dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}=\dfrac{-40}{-0.042}=952$ K. The reaction is spontaneous **below** 952 K.

questions.question: A soap micelle in water is shown. Identify which region, X or Y, is more polar.
questions.answer: **Y** (the water). X is the non-polar interior made of hydrocarbon tails.

questions.question: Fats are solid at room temperature and oils are generally liquids. Which of triglycerides A and B is more likely to be in oils and which in fats? Justify your choice.
questions.answer: A is more likely in a **fat** and B in an **oil**. B has more C=C double bonds, which put kinks in its chains. The molecules cannot pack as closely, so dispersion forces between them are weaker and the melting point is lower.

questions.question:
The effectiveness of a soap can be measured by its ability to froth in water. For each of three water sources, 1.0 mL of soap solution was added to 80.0 mL of water in one piece of glassware, which was sealed and shaken vigorously for 10 seconds. The total volume including froth was recorded.

| 2 | 89.0 | 86.0 | 86.0 | 87.0 |
| 3 | 82.0 | 82.0 | 84.0 | 82.7 |

State the independent variable.
questions.answer: The water source.

What piece of glassware would be used for these trials?

The effectiveness of a soap can be measured by its ability to froth in water. For each of three water sources, 1.0 mL of soap solution was added to 80.0 mL of water in one piece of glassware, which was sealed and shaken vigorously for 10 seconds. The total volume including froth was recorded.

From which water source is the soap least able to froth? Explain why.
questions.answer: **Source 3.** It is probably hard water containing $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions, which precipitate the soap anions as scum, leaving less soap to form froth.

questions.question:
Equal volumes of silver nitrate and sodium bromate solutions were mixed at 25 °C. The concentrations listed are those of the solutions before mixing.

| Test | $[\text{Ag}^+]$ (mol L$^{-1}$) | $[\text{BrO}_3^-]$ (mol L$^{-1}$) | Observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.05 | 0.05 | thick white precipitate |
| 2 | 0.025 | 0.05 | white precipitate |
| 3 | 0.005 | 0.05 | fine precipitate, settles |
| 4 | 0.0025 | 0.05 | fine precipitate, settles |
| 5 | 0.00125 | 0.05 | fine precipitate, settles |
| 6 | 0.0005 | 0.05 | no precipitate |
| 7 | 0.00025 | 0.05 | no precipitate |

Determine the range in which the solubility product of silver bromate must lie.
questions.answer:
Mixing equal volumes **halves** each concentration. $K_{sp}$ lies between the ion products of tests 5 and 6.

Test 5: $Q=(6.25\times10^{-4})(0.025)=1.56\times10^{-5}$. Test 6: $Q=(2.5\times10^{-4})(0.025)=6.25\times10^{-6}$.

So $6.3\times10^{-6}<K_{sp}<1.6\times10^{-5}$.

*Note: the school's solution did not halve the concentrations (giving $2.5\times10^{-5}$ to $6.3\times10^{-5}$).*

questions.question:
Equal volumes of silver nitrate and sodium bromate solutions were mixed at 25 °C. The concentrations listed are those of the solutions before mixing.

| Test | $[\text{Ag}^+]$ (mol L$^{-1}$) | $[\text{BrO}_3^-]$ (mol L$^{-1}$) | Observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.05 | 0.05 | thick white precipitate |
| 2 | 0.025 | 0.05 | white precipitate |
| 3 | 0.005 | 0.05 | fine precipitate, settles |
| 4 | 0.0025 | 0.05 | fine precipitate, settles |
| 5 | 0.00125 | 0.05 | fine precipitate, settles |
| 6 | 0.0005 | 0.05 | no precipitate |
| 7 | 0.00025 | 0.05 | no precipitate |

Use the average of the limits of the range for $K_{sp}$ (between tests 5 and 6) to estimate $K_{sp}$, then calculate the solubility of silver bromate.
questions.answer:
Allowing for the halving on mixing, the limits are $1.56\times10^{-5}$ and $6.25\times10^{-6}$, so the average is $K_{sp}\approx1.1\times10^{-5}$.

$s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}=3.3\times10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Write the molecular formula of cycasin, the toxin in cycads, shown here.
questions.answer: $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}\text{N}_2\text{O}_7$.

questions.question: Cycasin is the toxin in cycads. With reference to its structure and the equilibrium $\text{cycasin}(s)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{cycasin}(aq)$, explain using Le Chatelier's principle why leaving cycad material in running water for several days removes the toxin.
questions.answer:
Cycasin has several O–H groups and a polar N→O group, so it forms hydrogen bonds with water and is water soluble.

Running water continually carries away dissolved cycasin. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right to replace it, so more solid dissolves. Equilibrium is never established, and over several days nearly all the toxin is leached out.

questions.question: Draw (or give the structure of) a functional group isomer of cyclopentene.
questions.answer: A $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$ alkyne, e.g. pent-1-yne, $\text{CH}\equiv\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

questions.question: Write the chemical equation, using structural formulae, for the reaction of cyclopentene with bromine water.
questions.answer:
Addition across the double bond (the orange-brown colour fades). In water the major product is 2-bromocyclopentan-1-ol:

cyclo-$\text{C}_5\text{H}_8+\text{Br}_2(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightarrow$ cyclo-$\text{C}_5\text{H}_8\text{Br(OH)}+\text{HBr}(aq)$

HSC answers also accept simple addition: cyclopentene $+\text{Br}_2\rightarrow$ 1,2-dibromocyclopentane.

questions.question: Write a risk assessment for either cyclopentene or bromine water.
questions.answer:
**Cyclopentene:** highly flammable and harmful if inhaled; keep away from flames, use small quantities in a fume cupboard, and dispose into an organic waste container.

**Bromine water:** toxic vapour and corrosive to skin and eyes; use a fume cupboard, safety glasses and gloves.

questions.question: Hydrocyanic acid (HCN) is a weak acid. For a 2.2 M solution of HCN at 25 °C, you are given that its conjugate base $\text{CN}^-$ has $K_b=1.62\times10^{-5}$. Write the equation for the dissociation of HCN in water.
questions.answer: $\text{HCN}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{CN}^-(aq)$

questions.question: Hydrocyanic acid (HCN) is a weak acid. For a 2.2 M solution of HCN at 25 °C, you are given that its conjugate base $\text{CN}^-$ has $K_b=1.62\times10^{-5}$. Use an ICE table to find the equilibrium concentrations of all species in the dissociation (assume negligible dissociation).
questions.answer:
$K_a=\dfrac{10^{-14}}{1.62\times10^{-5}}=6.17\times10^{-10}$.

| | HCN | $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ | $\text{CN}^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | 2.2 | 0 | 0 |
| C | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| E | $2.2-x\approx2.2$ | $x$ | $x$ |

$x=\sqrt{6.17\times10^{-10}\times2.2}=3.7\times10^{-5}$.

$[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]=[\text{CN}^-]=3.7\times10^{-5}$ M and $[\text{HCN}]=2.2$ M.

*Note: the paper stated that the HCN solution "has a $K_b$ of $1.62\times10^{-5}$"; that constant belongs to $\text{CN}^-$.*

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the ball-and-stick model and the structural formula shown for representing ethane.
questions.answer:
**Ball-and-stick:** shows the three-dimensional tetrahedral arrangement, bond angles of about $109.5^\circ$ and rotation about C–C. However it exaggerates bond lengths, does not show electrons or true atomic sizes, needs a key for the elements, and is harder to draw.

**Structural formula:** quick to draw and clearly shows every atom (by symbol) and which atoms are bonded. However it is flat, suggesting $90^\circ$ angles, and gives no information about molecular shape or relative sizes.

questions.question: The mass spectrum of a hydrocarbon is shown. The hydrocarbon contains 85.7% C and 14.3% H by mass. Determine its molecular formula.
questions.answer:
$\text{C}:\text{H}=\dfrac{85.7}{12.01}:\dfrac{14.3}{1.008}=1:2$, so the empirical formula is $\text{CH}_2$ (14).

The molecular ion is at $m/z=112=8\times14$, so the formula is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}$.

questions.question: Give the structures of the two monomers that make up the polymer shown.
questions.answer: Benzene-1,4-diamine, $\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{NH}_2$, and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, $\text{HOOC}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COOH}$.

questions.question: What type of polymer is shown?
questions.answer: A condensation polymer (a polyamide).

questions.question: The polymer shown is very strong. Explain why, referring to its structure.
questions.answer: The polar N–H and C=O groups form many hydrogen bonds between neighbouring chains. The flat, rigid benzene rings keep the chains stiff and straight, so they pack closely and also attract strongly through dispersion forces.

questions.question: Outline the steps of a practical investigation to measure the enthalpy of neutralisation.
questions.answer:
1. Measure 25.0 mL of 1.0 M HCl into a polystyrene cup and 25.0 mL of 1.0 M NaOH into another vessel.
2. Allow both to reach the same temperature and record it.
3. Add the base to the acid, close the lid fitted with a thermometer, and stir.
4. Record the maximum temperature reached.
5. Calculate $q=mc\Delta T$ and divide by the moles of water formed. Repeat and average.

questions.question: 25.0 mL of 1.0 M acetic acid and 25.0 mL of 1.0 M NaOH are mixed and the temperature rises by 6.2 °C. Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation of acetic acid. (Assume the density of the mixture is 1 g mL$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
$q=mc\Delta T=50.0\times4.18\times6.2=1.30$ kJ.

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O})=0.025$ mol.

$\Delta H=-\dfrac{1.30}{0.025}=-52$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The concentration of a nitric acid solution was determined using 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the ammonia was placed in a conical flask with a few drops of methyl orange (giving a pale yellow colour) and titrated with the acid.

| Titration | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of $\text{HNO}_3$ (mL) | 37.8 | 36.1 | 36.2 | 36.0 |

Using this titration, explain the difference between the terms *equivalence point* and *end point*.
questions.answer: The **equivalence point** is when the moles of $\text{HNO}_3$ added equal the moles of $\text{NH}_3$ present (the 1:1 stoichiometric ratio). The **end point** is when methyl orange changes colour (yellow towards orange/red), which is observed and used to estimate the equivalence point.

questions.question:
The concentration of a nitric acid solution was determined using 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the ammonia was placed in a conical flask with a few drops of methyl orange (giving a pale yellow colour) and titrated with the acid.

| Titration | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of $\text{HNO}_3$ (mL) | 37.8 | 36.1 | 36.2 | 36.0 |

Write a balanced equation for the reaction.
questions.answer: $\text{HNO}_3(aq)+\text{NH}_3(aq)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3(aq)$

questions.question:
The concentration of a nitric acid solution was determined using 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the ammonia was placed in a conical flask with a few drops of methyl orange (giving a pale yellow colour) and titrated with the acid.

| Titration | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of $\text{HNO}_3$ (mL) | 37.8 | 36.1 | 36.2 | 36.0 |

Calculate the concentration of the acid.
questions.answer:
Excluding the outlier (37.8 mL), mean titre $=36.1$ mL.

$n(\text{NH}_3)=1.01\times0.02500=0.02525$ mol $=n(\text{HNO}_3)$.

$c=\dfrac{0.02525}{0.0361}=0.699$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
The concentration of a nitric acid solution was determined using 1.01 mol L$^{-1}$ ammonia. A 25.00 mL aliquot of the ammonia was placed in a conical flask with a few drops of methyl orange (giving a pale yellow colour) and titrated with the acid.

| Titration | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of $\text{HNO}_3$ (mL) | 37.8 | 36.1 | 36.2 | 36.0 |

Draw the expected titration curve (pH of the flask against volume of acid added). Label the axes.
questions.answer:
- Starts at about pH 11.6 (1.01 M weak base).
- Falls quickly at first, then gently through the buffer region.
- Steep drop around the equivalence point at 36.1 mL, where pH is about 4.8 (acidic because of $\text{NH}_4^+$).
- Levels off at low pH with excess strong acid.

*Note: the school's sketch started near pH 14, but 1.01 M ammonia has a pH of only about 11.6.*

questions.question: Name the three compounds shown, from top to bottom.
questions.answer:
1. 1,3-dibromo-1,1,3-trichloropropane
2. N,3-dimethylpentan-1-amine

questions.question: Compound Y, a colourless liquid with molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$, does not decolourise bromine water and does not produce $\text{CO}_2$ with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ solution. Its spectra are shown. Give the structural formula of Y, justifying your answer with reference to all three spectra.
questions.answer:
**Y is propan-2-yl ethanoate (isopropyl acetate), $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$.**

- No reaction with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ or bromine water: not a carboxylic acid and no C=C.
- **IR:** strong C=O near 1750 cm$^{-1}$ and C–O near 1250 cm$^{-1}$, with no broad O–H band: an ester.
- **$^{13}$C NMR:** four environments: 170 ppm (ester C=O), 68 ppm (C–O), 22 ppm (two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$) and 21 ppm ($\text{CH}_3$ on C=O).
- **$^1$H NMR:** 5.0 ppm septet, 1H: CH on oxygen with six neighbours. 2.0 ppm singlet, 3H: $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$. 1.2 ppm doublet, 6H: two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ next to one H.

questions.question: The diagram shows a reaction scheme that can be used to synthesise propanamide. Identify the reagents and conditions needed for steps 1–3, and explain how $^1$H NMR and mass spectrometry could be used to distinguish compounds M and O.
questions.answer:
- **Step 1:** concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat (dehydration).
- **Step 2:** water with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst, heat (hydration; gives mainly M with some O).
- **Step 3:** acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ (or $\text{KMnO}_4$), heat under reflux.

**Mass spectrometry:** both have $M^+$ at $m/z$ 60 but fragment differently. M (propan-2-ol) gives a major peak at 45 ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHOH}^+$, loss of $\text{CH}_3$); O (propan-1-ol) gives a major peak at 31 ($\text{CH}_2\text{OH}^+$).

**$^1$H NMR:** M has three environments (6H doublet, 1H multiplet, 1H OH singlet). O has four ($\text{CH}_3$ triplet, middle $\text{CH}_2$ multiplet, $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ triplet, OH singlet).

questions.question: The diagram shows a reaction scheme that can be used to synthesise propanamide. Give the structural formula of the organic product when compound P reacts with compound M.
questions.answer: Propan-2-yl propanoate: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$.

questions.question: The diagram shows a reaction scheme that can be used to synthesise propanamide. Compound P is reacted with compound M. How will the boiling point of the product compare with those of the reactants? Explain.
questions.answer: The ester (about 110 °C) boils **below propanoic acid** P (141 °C) but **above propan-2-ol** M (83 °C). P and M form hydrogen bonds between their molecules, while the ester has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces. That puts it below the acid; compared with the much smaller alcohol, its larger size (stronger dispersion forces) outweighs the lack of hydrogen bonding.\n\n*Note: the school said the ester boils lower than both reactants.*

questions.question: The diagram shows a reaction scheme that can be used to synthesise propanamide. Compound P is reacted with compound M to form an ester. Justify the equipment and conditions needed.
questions.answer:
- **Heating under reflux** (round-bottom flask, vertical condenser, heating mantle): heating speeds up the slow reaction, while the condenser returns volatile reactants and products without pressure building up.
- **Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$:** catalyst, and a dehydrating agent that shifts the equilibrium towards the ester.

questions.question:
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Standard $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ solutions gave these atomic absorption readings:

| $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (mg L$^{-1}$) | 0 | 50 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400 | 500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Absorbance | 0 | 0.060 | 0.120 | 0.240 | 0.360 | 0.480 | 0.600 |

Draw a labelled calibration curve of absorbance against concentration.
questions.answer: A straight line through the origin, with concentration on the horizontal axis (the dashed lines show a reading at absorbance 0.150).

questions.question:
Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Standard $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ solutions gave these atomic absorption readings:

| $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (mg L$^{-1}$) | 0 | 50 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400 | 500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Absorbance | 0 | 0.060 | 0.120 | 0.240 | 0.360 | 0.480 | 0.600 |

A 19.8 mg sample of the brass was dissolved in acid and made up to 100 mL. The absorbance of this solution was 0.150. Calculate the percentage by mass of copper in the brass.
questions.answer:
From the calibration line, $c=\dfrac{0.150}{0.0012}=125$ mg L$^{-1}$, so 100 mL contains 12.5 mg of Cu.

$\%\text{Cu}=\dfrac{12.5}{19.8}\times100=63.1\%$.
